# The skera cutting error

skera, PacBio's tool for splitting Kinnex HiFi reads into molecules, sometimes skips a real adapter and cuts at a look-alike sequence inside the next molecule. Every statement about skera below is marked as observed, with our numbers, or documented, with PacBio's words and the page they come from. Terms are defined in [concepts.md](concepts.md).

## What skera does

Observed on the three BD144 libraries (skera 26.1.0, the version that wrote our S-reads). In a complete array, skera sometimes passes over a real adapter and cuts instead at a sequence that resembles it inside the next molecule. Most often the skipped adapter is D (75% of the skipped adapters we find in ND). In 99% of those false cuts skera labels the cut with the letter of the adapter it skipped, so the S-read labels still run from A to Q in order and skera passes the read. The cut lies a median 891 bp further along the read than the skipped adapter.

Two S-reads come out wrong. The one before the false cut is a chimera: a whole molecule, the skipped adapter and the first part of the cut molecule. The one after it is a fragment, the rest of the cut molecule. On reads whose adapters run A to Q the fragment keeps the TSO end; on reads from the other strand (Q to A) it keeps the Read1 end, with the cell label. The chimera's other end sits at a real adapter in 98% of false cuts.

The read below, from ND, shows one false cut (`examples/example_reads.fasta`, record `skera_false_cut`; the coloured view is `examples/example_reads.html`). Uppercase marks the adapters and the site skera called D; positions are on the stretch of the read shown in the record.

```text
>skera_false_cut BD144_ND zm=1576268 read positions 2723-5795 of 14028 (adapter C to adapter E)
   1 ACTCTGTCAGGTCCGATctacacgacgctcttccgatctagatcggagcgtgatggagtcttgacaaggttctaggcaagcctttttttttttttttttt
     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ C 1-17: adapter C
...
1001 ccagggcctccgggcccccccgctgcaccggcgtcatccgccatttggtgttttgtcggaaaagaagcccatgtactctgcgttgataccactgcttACC
1101 TCCTCCTCCAGAATctacacgacgctcttccgatctccttcgaccgtgattgatgtatgacataccaggactcttccagttttttttttttttttttttt
     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ D(real) 1098-1114: the real adapter D, which skera skips (it starts on the line above)
...
2201 attaaccgcatattccttattatcaacatttccctgcgatttcttgcaatttGCATACTCCTCCAGAATtgcatctacatttttcttggcagggagttga
                                                         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ skera_D 2253-2269: the look-alike where skera cuts and writes D
```

## How we found it

The study does not use skera's cuts. It searches every HiFi read for the nine Kinnex adapters, the TSO and Read1 on both strands, and keeps an adapter hit only within 4 bp of a TSO or Read1 hit, where every real adapter sits (the full-read segmentation, `src/kinnex_qc`). Each S-read records where it lies in its HiFi read (the `qs` and `qe` tags, documented at https://skera.how/read-segments.html), so skera's cuts can be laid over ours read by read. In reads that skera passes, some gaps between consecutive S-reads have none of our adapters within 5 bp. We call each such gap a false cut.

For every false cut in complete arrays that skera passes we then looked up the molecule of ours that holds the cut, the adapter of ours left inside the neighbouring S-read (the one skera skipped), the end classes of the two S-reads, and whether lima, isoseq refine and mapping keep them (`study/analyses/false_cut_anatomy.py`).

On the calibration set, the first 200,000 HiFi reads of ND with their skera 26.1.0 S-reads, we aligned the sequence at each false cut to every Kinnex adapter (`study/analyses/false_cuts_calibration.py`). At 72% of false cuts it differs from D, its closest adapter, by 3 to 5 edits (an edit is one substituted, inserted or deleted base). Only 2.5% are within 2 edits of any adapter, the most our search accepts. A CTCCTCC repeat lies within 10 bp of 28%, so the look-alikes are not one fixed motif. The adapters skera skips match well: 99.9% of them are within 1 edit of the adapter and next to a TSO or Read1.

## How often

Observed, skera 26.1.0, hash samples of 18% of the ZMWs of each library; lima 2.13.0 in Iso-Seq mode:

| | ND | HM | kin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Complete arrays skera passes | 1,596,858 | 2,029,534 | 1,950,193 |
| False cuts in them | 142,451 | 178,916 | 175,319 |
| Complete arrays skera passes with at least one false cut | 8.7% | 8.6% | 8.8% |
| False cuts that skera labels D | 74% | 74% | 74% |
| False cuts where we find the real adapter skera skipped | 99.6% | 99.6% | 99.6% |
| Of those, the skipped adapter is D | 75% | 75% | 74% |
| Of those, skera labels the cut with the skipped adapter's letter | 99% | 99% | 99% |
| Of those, lima passes the chimera | 0.4% | 0.4% | 0.3% |
| Of those, lima passes the fragment | 0.0% | 0.0% | 0.0% |
| Median distance from the skipped adapter to the cut (bp) | 891 | 890 | 899 |
| lima passes the proper S-reads of these arrays, for comparison | 99.9% | 100.0% | 100.0% |

With or without TSO-TSO depletion, false cuts turn up in all three libraries alike, in 8.6% to 8.8% of the complete arrays that skera passes. Source data: `report/tables/fig1_skera_false_cut_anatomy.tsv`, behind Supplementary Fig. 1 of the Note.

## What it costs

Observed: lima passes 0.0% of the fragments and 0.3% to 0.4% of the chimeras, against 99.9% or more of proper S-reads. Each false cut therefore costs two molecules in the standard workflow (skera, lima, isoseq refine, mapping): the cut one and the whole one fused to it. In kin, the library with the Kinnex TSO artifact removal, that comes to 0.17 molecules per HiFi read, most of the 0.18 usable molecules per read that skera does not write as a clean S-read. Cutting every read at our own adapters keeps 7.86 molecules per kin HiFi read, against 7.68 with the standard workflow (Supplementary Fig. 6).

Our own segmentation has a smaller weakness: it misses an adapter that skera finds in 0.15% to 0.18% of the reads skera passes, mostly the A or Q at the end of a read.

## What PacBio documents

What skera does, from its documentation at https://skera.how/:

> Skera splits Kinnex HiFi reads at adapter positions generating segmented reads (S-reads).

How it is told which adapters to look for, https://skera.how/adapters.html:

> Adapters must be in FASTA format `<adapters>.fasta` and ordered in the expected order of adapters in the reads. There should be one entry per adapter (forward or reverse-complement orientation) with no overlapping adapter sequences. Duplicate names or sequences are not allowed.

What goes into its two output files, https://skera.how/output.html:

> Skera outputs a BAM file containing all segmented reads that have sequential leading and trailing adapters based on the order of adapters in the input fasta.

> The non_passing.bam file contains the bam records that have adapters found in non-sequential order. This file is necessary for skera undo.

In pbbioconda issue 608, opened about skera 1.1.0 because some reads were in both files, a contributor to PacBio's repository replied on 2023-09-19 that `non_passing.bam` holds the HiFi record of every read whose adapter array skera did not find in full, so that `skera undo` can run, and gave this example (https://github.com/PacificBiosciences/pbbioconda/issues/608#issuecomment-1726413858):

> For example, if `skera` finds 14 / 15 expected segments(fragments), the 14 expected segments will be output to the segmented read output _and_ the HiFi input read will be output to the `non_passing` bam.

skera 1.2.0 (bioconda pbskera 1.2.0) lists these options in `skera split --help`, none of them about how adapters are matched; skera 1.4.0 lists the same:

```
  -h,--help               Show this help and exit.
  --version               Show application version and exit.
  -j,--num-threads  INT   Number of threads to use, 0 means autodetection. [0]
  --log-level       STR   Set log level. Valid choices: (TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, FATAL). [WARN]
  --log-file        FILE  Log to a file, instead of stderr.
```

What these pages do not say (read on 2026-11-05): how many mismatches or edits skera accepts when it matches an adapter, whether it looks at the sequence around a match, or what it does with mirror arrays. The changelog (https://skera.how/changelog.html) has no entry about adapter matching and none for 26.1.0; its latest entry, 26.2.0, adds a "minimum segmented read length filter". We do not have skera 26.1.0 itself; our S-reads came from it as delivered with the data.

## How to check your data and recover the molecules

Run `kinnex-qc` on the HiFi BAM with skera's S-reads:

```
kinnex-qc run --hifi hifi_reads.bam --sreads segmented.bam --out qc/
```

Section 4 of `qc/report.html` gives the share of complete arrays skera passes that have at least one false cut, the letter skera gave each false cut and the letter of the adapter it skipped, with a drawing of one false cut; section 5 shows example reads from your data, one of them with a false cut when a read qualifies. The numbers are in `qc/summary.json` under `skera` (`false_cut_reads_share`, `false_cuts`, `false_cut_letters`, `skipped_adapter_letters`), and `qc/reads.tsv.gz` has a `false_cuts` column per read. `kinnex-qc` does not run lima, so it counts false cuts but not their lima verdicts.

To recover the molecules, add `--write-molecules`:

```
kinnex-qc run --hifi hifi_reads.bam --sreads segmented.bam --write-molecules --out qc/
```

`qc/molecules.bam` then holds one unaligned record per usable molecule (TSO at one end, Read1 at the other, nothing fused) of every read in the BAM, not only the sampled ones, cut at our adapters and carrying the header and read group of `segmented.bam` (or of `--template`), so that lima takes each record as an S-read. Use it in place of `segmented.bam`: it holds the molecules skera writes cleanly as well as the ones around false cuts and on the unwritten arms of mirror arrays. For FLIGHT-seq cDNA, with the primers the study used (`resources/primers_FlashBD.fasta`):

```
lima --isoseq --peek-guess qc/molecules.bam resources/primers_FlashBD.fasta qc/molecules.isoseq.bam
isoseq refine qc/molecules.isoseq.FlashBD_5p--FlashBD_3p.bam resources/primers_FlashBD.fasta qc/molecules.flnc.bam
```

Then map the fltnc reads as usual. In the study's test on ND (`study/analyses/downstream_test.py`, lima 2.13.0, isoseq refine 4.3.0, minimap2 2.30), molecules that skera never wrote, cut at our coordinates from mirror reads, passed lima in 99.8% of cases, refine in 99.8% and mapping in 99.1%, against 99.9%, 99.9% and 99.1% for molecules of complete reads. That test used molecules of mirror and complete reads, not the molecules around false cuts in particular.
